idiom_name: apicache full-response middleware, or Cache-Control + a shared cache in front
implementation_notes: In Express/Node the page cache is a middleware that stores the whole response - status, headers and body - and replays it: apicache.middleware('5 minutes') mounted app-wide, or apicache('10 minutes') per route, keeps entries in process memory by default, can be pointed at Redis so several processes share them, respects Cache-Control request directives (no-store/no-cache bypass), and can write the matching Cache-Control header itself. Where a CDN or nginx already sits in front, the JS layer contributes only the contract instead of the bytes: setting Cache-Control (s-maxage for shared caches, plus stale-while-revalidate), Vary and ETag and letting the shared cache hold the page, which is the usual choice for marketing or documentation pages because it survives restarts and deploy-time purges. Both are library-level realizations - nothing in Node's core caches responses.
pitfalls: The default store is per-process memory, so with several workers or a container restart the cache is partial or empty - configure Redis before quoting a hit ratio.
Middleware mounted before authentication caches everything, including personalised responses; mount per route after the auth middleware, or add an explicit no-store bypass for those routes.
Invalidation is the weak spot: apicache.clear() reaches only the entries that process (or its Redis keys) knows about, so a purge that must also hit a CDN or edge needs a separate purge call.
